text.p: The following are the main stories from Thursday morning's German newspapers:
FRANKFURTER ALLGEMEINE ZEITUNG

- Bonn decides on the slaughter of more than 5,000 cows imported from Switzerland and Britain. Farmers to receive 1,500 to 2,000 marks compensation per animal. Around 14,000 offspring of the imported cattle are to be put under watch.
- Tax reform commission decides that pensions should be taxed at half the current rate in the future.

- Christian Social Union (CSU) want the German-Czech reconciliation accord signed in Prague on Tuesday to be discussed in parliament on January 30, to make clear that the document is not a "final stroke."
- Dollar reaches 1.64 marks.
- Continuing guessing about the Germany's Transrapid high -speed train. Rumours that the project may have abandoned.
HANDELSBLATT
- Coalition decides on major tax reform, the details of which are due to be announced later on Thursday. But the question of how much value-added tax should be raised is not tackled.
- Security for exporters extended. State security for exports should be extended to joint exports from German and foreign companies in third countries.
- German Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt starts competition offensive in electricity and gas markets, speaking at the Handelsblatt energy business forum on Wednesday.
- After the first case of mad cow disease in a cow born in Germany, 5,200 cows to be killed.
SUEDDEUTSCHE ZEITUNG

- Junior coalition partners the Free Democrats (FDP) sees itself as winner in tax reform dispute as coalition announces agreement on package including income tax cuts, demanded by FDP. But higher value-added taxes still disputed.
- Slaughter of 5,200 cows agreed after latest BSE case.
- Hanover plans all-women's university to open in three years time, to be called The Virginia Woolf University.
- Social costs paid by employers and employees have risen by almost 50 percent since 1991, according to the Institute of the German Economy.
- Anti-nuclear power campaigners lose their case to have the oldest nuclear plant in Germany at Obrigheim shut down.
DIE WELT
- Coalition unite over tax reform plans.
- Slaughter of 5,200 cows. But Health Minister Jochen Borchert sees no danger for consumers.
- Opponents of Obrigheim nuclear plant loose case to have power plant shut down.
- Relationships with Turkey damaged as Frankfurt court accuses the Turkish government of links to the international heroin trade.
